To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the spinal cord is necessary for locomotion, 2) the spinal cord can be partially lesioned and still produce locomotion, 3) locomotion can be partially recovered after complete transection of the spinal cord, and 4) the recovery of locomotion after complete spinal transection is not due to a spared ventrolateral spinal pathway.

5 of 10 monkeys with complete spinal cord lesions (transected at T8) exhibited locomotor movements postoperatively and that the monkeys' hind limbs commonly exhibited increased interlimb cycle durations postoperatively.

1) the primate spinal cord is less able to organize locomotion than the spinal cord of lower mammals, and 2) the primate's ability to locomote after spinal cord injury may be greater than previously believed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying recovery from spinal cord injuries in monkeys.
the study of the neural basis of movement and behavior.
the study of the neural basis of locomotor behavior in the monkey and with the development of a model for the study of locomotor recovery in man.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the primate's capacity for locomotor recovery is limited by the extent of the cord lesion.
the primate's capacity to recover locomotion after partial spinal cord lesions is not significantly different from that of the rat, cat, and dog.
, although the spinal cord of the primate is capable of generating locomotor movements, it seems less able to do so than the cord of other mammals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the primate's locomotor system is less able to compensate for significant lesions of the spinal cord than that of other mammals.
the primate's ability to recover locomotion after a spinal cord lesion may not be as impaired as previously believed.
the primate's locomotor system, although not as readily organized as in lower mammals, does have some ability to organize and execute locomotor movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can see the spinal cord can recover from a lesion.
the spinal cord of primates can generate locomotor movements in the absence of descending input.
the primate spinal cord is not the only determinant of locomotor behavior, and that the primate locomotor pattern is not necessarily the same as in other mammals.
